nameStory: The "pileated" in this woodpecker's name comes from the Latin word "pileus," meaning a felt cap worn in ancient Rome. This refers to the bird's striking bright red crest that sits atop its head like a tall, pointed hat. Early naturalists thought this prominent red "cap" was the bird's most distinctive feature, and the name has stuck for centuries.
description: The Pileated Woodpecker is New England's largest woodpecker, roughly the size of a crow with a dramatic appearance that's hard to miss. Its body is mostly black with bold white stripes running down its neck, but the real showstopper is its bright red crest that stands tall like a mohawk. Both males and females sport this impressive red headgear, though males have an additional red stripe on their cheek. These powerful birds are famous for their rectangular excavations in dead trees, which look almost like someone took a chisel to the bark.

idTips.label: Bright Red Crest
idTips.description: A tall, pointed red cap that stands prominently above the head - impossible to miss and visible even from a distance. The crest feathers can be raised or lowered depending on the bird's mood.

idTips.label: Crow-Sized Body
idTips.description: Much larger than other woodpeckers - about the size of a crow with a long neck and substantial build. When flying, their size alone distinguishes them from smaller woodpeckers.

idTips.label: White Neck Stripes
idTips.description: Bold white stripes run from the bill down the sides of the neck, creating a striking contrast against the black body. These stripes are visible both when the bird is on a tree and in flight.

idTips.label: Rectangular Holes
idTips.description: Look for large, almost perfectly rectangular cavities chiseled into dead or dying trees - these are the pileated's calling cards. The holes are much larger and more geometric than those made by other woodpeckers.

idTips.label: Undulating Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a distinctive up-and-down roller coaster pattern, flapping a few times then folding wings to glide. Their large size makes this undulating flight very noticeable.

idTips.label: Loud Drumming
idTips.description: Produces powerful, resonant drumming that can be heard from great distances - much louder and deeper than smaller woodpeckers. The sound echoes through the forest like someone hammering on a hollow tree.

habitat: Pileated Woodpeckers prefer mature deciduous and mixed forests with plenty of large, dead or dying trees throughout New England. You'll find them in both deep woods and forest edges, particularly where there are standing snags (dead trees) that harbor the insects they love to eat. They're equally at home in maple-oak forests, mixed pine-hardwood areas, and even wooded suburban areas with large trees.

seasonality.spring: Most active and vocal during breeding season, with frequent drumming and calling echoing through the woods. Look for fresh rectangular excavations as they prepare nesting cavities in dead trees.
seasonality.summer: Quieter as they focus on raising young, but still visible foraging on dead wood. Parent birds can be seen carrying food to nest holes in large snags.
seasonality.fall: Often seen in small family groups as young birds learn to forage. Fresh wood chips scattered at the base of trees indicate recent pileated activity.
seasonality.winter: More likely to visit bird feeders with suet, and their tracks and rectangular holes in snow-covered logs are easier to spot. Their loud calls carry further through bare winter woods.

funFact: A single Pileated Woodpecker can excavate a nest cavity so large that Wood Ducks, owls, and even flying squirrels will move in after they're done - making them like the forest's construction crew, building apartments for dozens of other species throughout their lifetime!
confusionNotes: The only bird that might cause confusion is the much rarer Ivory-billed Woodpecker, but that species is likely extinct and was never common in New England. Remember: if you see a huge woodpecker with a red crest in New England, it's definitely a Pileated - they're the only game in town at that size!
contextualKnowledge: Many people mispronounce this bird's name - it can be said either "PY-lee-ay-ted" or "PIL-ee-ay-ted," and both are considered correct by ornithologists. The Pileated Woodpecker was actually the inspiration for the famous cartoon character Woody Woodpecker, though the cartoon version was given a more exaggerated appearance and personality.
compareHints: Since there are no other Dryocopus species in New England, compare the Pileated to other large woodpeckers like the Northern Flicker, which is much smaller, brownish, and lacks the red crest. The Red-headed Woodpecker is also smaller with an entirely red head (not just a crest) and more white on the body. No other New England woodpecker comes close to the Pileated's impressive size and distinctive rectangular excavations.
